issue: ApiHelper.validateResponseErrorCode read node.has("success") in camelCase; lowercase 'success' occurs in 0 of 1,868 measured responses and PascalCase 'Success' in 1,580. Jackson is case-sensitive, so the framework's only application-envelope assertion could never pass.
recommended_solution: Delegate all envelope field access to a single normalisation class (PamEnvelope) that resolves either casing, unwraps a one-element array only when it is genuinely an envelope, and classifies the response shape. DONE this objective.
recommended_advantages: One place to fix casing and shape variance forever; every consumer benefits at once; verified against 8 real shape classes by 15 passing tests; makes the 31-shape problem tractable.
recommended_disadvantages: Adds a class between the test and the response, so a reader must know it exists. Slightly more indirection when debugging a single assertion.
alternative_solution: Patch the string literals in place - change "success" to "Success" and add a fallback for each field.
alternative_advantages: Minimal diff, no new classes, trivially reviewable.
alternative_disadvantages: Fixes only casing, not the 31 shapes. Would still fail on bare arrays, object-valued Result and the 288 responses with no Success field, and the same bug would recur in the next method that parses a body by hand.

issue: The framework validated HTTP status codes on an API where a rejected request normally returns HTTP 200 with the rejection in the body. Status-only assertions scored the 2026-07-29 run 90% green against a true 64%, and caught 0 of 70 responses where Success:true accompanied no write.
recommended_solution: Adopt a layered validator (PamApiValidator, L1-L12) that runs every configured layer, collects outcomes, and asserts once at the end - with NOT_RUN as a first-class verdict so unmet layers are counted rather than absorbed. DONE this objective; migrate the 76 existing API suites onto it controller by controller.
recommended_advantages: One call yields a full picture instead of stopping at the first shallow failure; the coverage gap becomes countable; layers L1-L7 match the chaining harness so framework and harness results compare directly; catches the Already Exists trap, which nothing previously did.
recommended_disadvantages: Migration touches every API test. Tests become more verbose at the call site, and layers L9-L12 will mostly report NOT_RUN until the contract exists, which can look like the tool is not working.
recommended_effort: M - framework 2 days (complete); suite migration 10-15 days
alternative_solution: Add an envelope assertion to the existing validate* methods without restructuring - one extra check on Success plus Message inside each current method.
alternative_advantages: No migration; existing tests gain envelope checking immediately; far smaller change to review.
alternative_disadvantages: Still fails on the first problem, so shallow failures continue to mask deep ones. No way to distinguish 'not checked' from 'checked and passed', which is precisely the flaw that produced the misleading L6 read-back figures. No path to schema, persistence or security layers.

issue: KNOWN_ERROR_CODES was hardcoded to {201,202,203} and asserted hard, so the real measured ErrorCode 206-LC_GLD on HTTP 200 would have been reported as a broken test. No product error-code registry exists to validate against - 4 codes are documented for 1,306 endpoints.
recommended_solution: Replace with an extensible ErrorCodeRegistry that matches on the numeric prefix (codes carry module suffixes) and records an unrecognised code as an observation rather than a failure. DONE this objective.
recommended_advantages: Stops misreporting legitimate product responses as test defects; accumulates a real registry from evidence; surfaces unknown codes as a list to hand to development, which is the actual fix.
recommended_disadvantages: A genuinely wrong error code is no longer caught automatically unless the test states the expected one explicitly. Trades some strictness for correctness, which must be understood by whoever reads the reports.
alternative_solution: Keep the hard assertion but externalise the code set to a properties file that testers extend as codes are found.
alternative_advantages: Retains strict failure on unexpected codes; no code change needed to add a code.
alternative_disadvantages: Every newly encountered legitimate code fails a build until someone edits the file, so the suite generates false failures indefinitely - and blames the product for undocumented behaviour by failing the test rather than reporting the gap.

issue: Database validation had never run and could not have. AutoConfigs.db_name read the property key "databaseName" and db_user_name read "db_user" - neither key existed in any environment file, so both resolved to null. db_type was the hardcoded literal "mysql" while DBUtils built a jdbc:sqlserver URL. DBUtils had zero callers and every method returned void or printed to stdout.
recommended_solution: Rewrite DBUtils: dialect derived from db_type, query() returning materialised rows, assertion-shaped helpers (count/exists/queryScalar/queryFirstRow), PreparedStatement binding, try-with-resources, and read-only by default with any non-SELECT refused unless allowMutations() is called explicitly. Read config keys canonically with a fallback to the historic spellings. DONE and verified end to end against QA.
recommended_advantages: Enables L11 persistence assertions at all; the read-only guard bounds the blast radius of a sysadmin credential; backward compatible with the historic property spellings that upstream had just populated, so nothing breaks; verified by executing the exact JDBC URL the framework builds.
recommended_disadvantages: Reads config from two possible key names, which is mild ambiguity that should be collapsed once the environment files are standardised.
alternative_solution: Rename the keys in all 20 environment files to match what AutoConfigs already read, and leave DBUtils printing to stdout.
alternative_advantages: Smallest possible change to make a connection open; touches no Java logic.
alternative_disadvantages: A connection that opens is not validation - no assertion could consume a result, so no test would be able to check persistence. Leaves the mysql/sqlserver contradiction in place and provides no safety guard against a sysadmin credential.

issue: The negative API suite is largely non-functional and the working part tests the opposite of its name. 199 of 279 referenced @DataProvider names do not exist, so 650 @Test methods fail at TestNG initialisation; all 80 providers that resolve read the POSITIVE data sheets. Separately the 3,652-row negative workbook is declared in AutoConfigs and set in 6 environment files but read by no provider.
recommended_solution: Triage in three passes: delete tests referencing providers that will never exist, re-point the remaining classes at negative data, then add assertions via PamApiValidator. Report no negative coverage figure until pass two completes.
recommended_advantages: Removes actively misleading tests first, which is the highest-value step; no developer dependency; leaves a small honest suite rather than a large false one; the authored negative data becomes reachable.
recommended_disadvantages: Headline test counts will fall sharply, which needs explaining to stakeholders who have seen the larger number. Requires per-class judgement rather than a mechanical fix.
alternative_solution: Generate the missing 199 data providers mechanically from the negative workbook's sheet names, wiring each class to the correspondingly named negative sheet.
alternative_advantages: Restores the whole suite to runnable in one pass; makes the unread workbook reachable; largely scriptable.
alternative_disadvantages: Mechanically wiring 199 providers will produce tests that run but assert only 405/401 - 2 of 19 categories - so it converts non-functional tests into shallow ones and re-establishes a large green suite that still proves little. It also assumes sheet names correspond to class names, which is unverified.

issue: The chaining harness recorded 105 of 107 L6 read-backs as FAIL when 97 of them could never have passed: store() refuses a None so NEW_ID never entered vars, substitute() returned the placeholder unchanged (chain_runner.py:200), and value_anywhere() guards only against empty and 'none' (chain_runner.py:529) - so the check deep-searched each response for the literal string ${NEW_ID}.
recommended_solution: Make an unresolved placeholder a distinct outcome: detect that substitution did not resolve, skip the check, and record NOT RUN with the reason instead of FAIL. Mirror the framework's ValidationOutcome semantics.
recommended_advantages: Stops the harness manufacturing product failures out of its own missing inputs; makes the read-back figures meaningful; aligns harness and framework verdict vocabularies so results compare; 2 known false negatives disappear.
recommended_disadvantages: Reported FAIL counts drop, which will look like coverage regressed when in fact accuracy improved - needs a note in the next run report.
alternative_solution: Guard value_anywhere() against any string still containing a ${...} token, failing loudly at the point of substitution instead.
alternative_advantages: Very small change; catches the whole class of unresolved-placeholder bugs anywhere in the harness, not just L6.
alternative_disadvantages: Fails the flow rather than marking the single check NOT RUN, so it loses the surrounding layers' results for that hop and still cannot distinguish a harness gap from a product defect in the report.

issue: Two latent defects that bite exactly when the suite is scaled to the full endpoint catalogue: APIExcelReportUtil increments a static int rowIndex with no synchronisation while API suites run parallel='classes', and ApiHelper calls Playwright.create() per request without ever closing the instances.
recommended_solution: Make the row index an AtomicInteger (or synchronise the append), and close each Playwright instance in a finally block or reuse one per thread via ThreadLocal.
recommended_advantages: Small, self-contained, no developer dependency, and it protects report integrity precisely when coverage is scaled up - the worst moment to lose trust in the evidence.
recommended_disadvantages: Touches ApiHelper, the highest-blast-radius file in the repo, so it needs an impact check and a full regression pass.
alternative_solution: Run API suites single-threaded and accept the resource leak for the duration of a run.
alternative_advantages: Zero code change; removes the data race immediately by removing concurrency.
alternative_disadvantages: A full-catalogue run already took 11,503 s with concurrency; serialising it makes routine execution impractical. The Playwright leak is unaffected and worsens with request count.

issue: The bearer token committed to Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties expired 2026-07-31, tokens last 24 hours, and the GenericScheduler service account that issues them is locked - and is also the data-warehouse ETL account, so a test-side lockout became an ETL outage.
recommended_solution: Provision a dedicated automation service account, separate from ETL, and read the token from an environment variable or CI secret at run time rather than from a committed file.
recommended_advantages: Removes the cross-domain blast radius immediately - a test lockout can no longer stop ETL; takes a credential out of version control; makes unattended scheduled runs possible for the first time.
recommended_disadvantages: Requires IT Operations action, so QA cannot deliver it alone.
recommended_effort: S - 1 day of IT work, plus 0.5 day framework
alternative_solution: Keep the shared account but never call /arcontoken from automation - have the owner issue a token manually per run and export it as PAM_API_TOKEN.
alternative_advantages: Available today with no dependency; already the working practice; guarantees the lockout cannot deepen.
alternative_disadvantages: Requires a human before every run, so scheduled or CI-triggered regression remains impossible, and any run longer than 24 hours fails mid-flight. It manages the symptom and leaves the shared-account risk in place.

issue: Three catalogue defects in APIConfig.java: a double-slash typo at line 188 drops the real endpoint AzureKeyVault/GetDatabaseStatus from the canonical count; 'Se0rviceDetailsV3' is a typo producing a hard 404; and the SCIM root User/ is declared three times. Separately, 210 endpoints present in the positive Excel are absent from APIConfig.java, 7 data providers reference non-existent Excel tables, and 9 of 79 positive classes are in no suite.
recommended_solution: Fix all catalogue defects in one deliberate change, republish the canonical count with its derivation, and add a CI check that reconciles APIConfig.java against the Excel corpus and the suite XMLs.
recommended_advantages: The reconciliation check prevents recurrence, which is the real value - these defects were invisible because nothing compared the three sources. Fixing them together means the count changes exactly once.
recommended_disadvantages: Changing the canonical count invalidates cross-references in every existing report, so it needs coordinated documentation updates in the same change.
alternative_solution: Fix only the two typos now and leave the count at 1,306, documenting the discrepancy.
alternative_advantages: Removes the hard 404 and the dropped endpoint immediately without disturbing any published figure.
alternative_disadvantages: The three-way inconsistency between catalogue, Excel and suites persists undetected, and the 210 uncatalogued endpoints stay invisible to any coverage measurement.

issue: The supplied QA database login (devops) is sysadmin and dbcreator over 30 databases, several of them not QA, and it is committed in plaintext to the environment file - as are the credentials in all 20 environment files. The database also stores API passwords in cleartext, so read access there is credential access.
recommended_solution: Issue a least-privilege login scoped to ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA with SELECT only (DDL provided in docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md section 6.1), and move all credentials to a secret store or CI-injected variables.
recommended_advantages: Bounds the blast radius by permission rather than by convention; removes secrets from version control; a SELECT-only account cannot damage data even if a script is wrong.
recommended_disadvantages: Requires DBA and IT Operations action; secret injection needs a small change to how local runs are configured, which adds friction for developers.
recommended_effort: S - 1-2 days across DBA and QA
alternative_solution: Keep the credential but rely on the code-level guard - DBUtils refuses any non-SELECT statement unless allowMutations() is called, and requests driver-level read-only (accepted by the SQL Server driver, verified).
alternative_advantages: Already in place and verified today; no external dependency; two independent layers of guard.
alternative_disadvantages: A guard in code is bypassable by any other tool, script or ad-hoc query using the same credential - and the credential remains in version control. It reduces the chance of an accident but not the authority to cause one.
